FROM A SEASON RECORD TO A WIN CHANCE

Where every number comes from.

Three different things power this model: observed data, relationships fitted to that data, and chosen assumptions. Everything runs in your browser using bundled snapshots; there is no live odds feed.

  1. Read the season record. NBA, MLB and NFL use wins divided by games. NHL uses standings points divided by 2 × games; Premier League uses earned points divided by 3 × matches. Their slider limits are 82 wins, 168 points, 162 wins, 17 wins and 114 points respectively.
  2. Find its place in league history. Compare the win or points percentage with the latest 20 eligible completed seasons in that sport. A smoothed historical percentile becomes an internal strength proxy. This translation is a modeling choice: an equally rare NBA and NFL season need not reflect equal true ability.
  3. Turn the strength gap into game odds. NBA, NHL, MLB and NFL use regular-season games across all teams, excluding every head-to-head meeting from the season-end strength records. Premier League uses season-end points, excluding both head-to-head meetings, to estimate win/draw/loss retrospectively. Changing the rules can change how much the same strength gap matters.
  4. Play out the format. Calculate scores, ties and best-of-series outcomes. Then sample up to 100,000 matchups. More trials make the simulation steadier; they do not make the assumptions more realistic.
Inspect every sport’s starting numbers

The opportunity counts and scoring-reward mixes are simplified choices, not measured possession/shot/drive datasets. All five baseline mean scores are calculated from historical results. Scoring-event probabilities are derived to reproduce those means. That does not validate opportunity counts, score-margin distributions or the effects of rule changes.

Inspect the fitted coefficients and other assumptions

Other chosen constants: controlled mechanics use a 0.12 strength coefficient. Game-day form adds −0.24, −0.12, 0, +0.12 or +0.24 to the relative scoring log-odds, with probabilities 6.25%, 25%, 37.5%, 25% and 6.25%. Both are assumptions, not estimated from game-level scoring data.

Default controls: scoring, opportunities, sensitivity and form are 1×; extra event volatility, home advantage and rest edge are 0. The base scoring-event rate is capped at 95% for extreme experiments. Event volatility redistributes rewards to zero/base/double while keeping their mean unchanged. Home and rest sliders are hypothetical log-odds adjustments, not measured points or days.

Format: one game or best of 3/5/7; stop as soon as a team clinches. Single Premier League matches retain draws. Other formats use fair 50–50 deciders for model ties. Games are independent across a hypothetical series; actual overtime and penalties are not modeled.

Simulation: 10,000 trials and seed 42 are reproducibility defaults. Headline odds are calculated directly; squares and counts are simulated. The 95% Wilson interval uses the standard 1.96 normal quantile and covers simulation error only. It does not include uncertainty in the fitted coefficients or model design.

Historical outcome checks: all five sports

Real game outcomes now anchor every league’s baseline. Coverage and evidence differ, so each fit is shown with its own check. Lookback accuracy is not forecasting accuracy.

Where does the data come from?

Bundled historical snapshots ground the record sliders: NBA rarity standings directly from ESPN, with game-fit snapshots from SportsDataverse’s ESPN collection; NHL and MLB records from their official statistics APIs; NFL results from nflverse; and Premier League results from OpenFootball. The sources, sample sizes and exclusions below are part of the model. Nothing loads live while you run an experiment.

We go back until each league has 20 eligible completed regular seasons. The reference excludes 2019–20 and 2020–21 for NBA, NHL and Premier League, and 2020 for MLB and NFL. 2021 MLB and NFL are included. Canceled or shortened lockout seasons and incomplete team records are handled in the table above. MLB’s completed 2026 regular season is included; NFL’s ongoing 2026 season is not.

Rarity history and game evidence answer different questions. These 20 seasons determine how unusual your chosen record is. The game-outcome fits below still use their separate ten-season samples, including COVID years; the expanded rarity scale does not add more game outcomes. Validation uses only rarity records available by its training cutoff.

Use the record fans recognize.

NBA, MLB and NFL use season wins. NHL uses standings points: 2 for a win, 1 for an overtime or shootout loss. Premier League uses earned season points: 3 for a win, 1 for a draw. Soccer points are calculated before administrative deductions so the scale reflects on-field results; they can differ from the published table for a penalized club.

The NHL reference reaches 2002–03 and 2003–04, when tied games also earned one point. Those seasons predate shootouts, so this broad sample mixes points-awarding eras. NHL’s current 84-game schedule allows 168 points. We compare the selected share of available points against 82-game historical seasons; 100 points today means 100/168, not 100/164. Premier League allows 114 points across 38 matches. Season points describe the record, while both sports’ game-score charts remain in goals.

The rarity readout counts team-seasons at or above that selected pace. Zero examples means “not observed in this sample,” not impossible. Extreme records keep their selected value while the modeled strength is capped.

One matchup. Two sides of the odds.

Team A and Team B each have their own league and season-record slider. Choose a 50-win NBA team and a 10-win NFL team, then choose the rules they both play under. The headline is a direct hypothetical matchup: Team A wins, Team B wins and (for a single Premier League match) a draw total 100%. Changing either record changes both odds.

We translate each source record to relative strength using its historical rarity, then apply the selected sport’s model. This compares hypothetical teams of equivalent standing; it does not model basketball players learning football. Cross-sport translation is an assumption, even when the selected league baseline uses historical game results.

The main probabilities are exact model odds. The outcome grid and win counts come from one shared set of simulated matchups, with shared A/B outcomes and explicit draws for a single Premier League match. Other formats use fair deciders for model ties. Neutral venues, equal rest and one game are the default.

The alternative rules result keeps both teams fixed and changes the sport, format or context. “Separate benchmark matchups,” under Comparison options, retains the earlier view for saved experiments: each team faces a typical opponent in its own league, and those independent probabilities need not sum to 100%.

Match rarity, or match record percentage.

Historical rarity compares similarly unusual records in each league’s own win or points distribution. Equivalent records can be fractional and are marked ≈; changing the league preserves that translated pace, while moving the slider selects whole wins or points. Record percentage keeps the same fraction of available wins or points: 50% means winning half the games in NBA/MLB/NFL, earning half the available standings points in NHL, or half the available points in Premier League. These are distinct record measures; equal percentages need not imply equally strong seasons.

We interpolate smoothed historical midranks into a latent strength proxy: θ = logit(rank). This gives familiar records a consistent internal scale. Rarity is not itself the chance of winning a matchup, nor proof that teams of equal rarity have equal true ability. Outside the observed range we cap the strength proxy at the nearest observed endpoint and flag the limitation.

How history changes the baseline odds.

NBA, NHL and NFL learn from regular-season games across all teams, including those that missed the playoffs: 11,979 NBA games, 12,200 NHL games and 2,614 decisive NFL games. For each matchup, remove every regular-season meeting between those two clubs from both final records. The remaining results against other opponents supply strength. NBA/NFL use wins; NHL uses actual standings points, including overtime and shootout rules. This is a season-end lookback with hindsight, not a pregame forecast.

A fitted home term separates venue effects; neutral simulations remove it. Nine NFL ties remain in season-record denominators but are excluded as binary outcomes. NFL odds select a winner; they do not estimate the chance of a real regular-season tie.

Playoffs are checked separately using earlier regular-season records. An earlier-playoff fit is also shown as a comparison, but no automatic playoff adjustment is applied. Best-of-series odds combine the regular-season game model with independent games. The checks below separately show games involving teams that missed the playoffs, including subgroups where the model did not beat the simple home-only baseline.

MLB now uses the same completed-season question as NBA and NHL: how does the record against other opponents relate to winning this matchup? All direct meetings are removed. The fit covers 22,762 decisive regular-season games; one tied game stays in record denominators but is excluded as a target. The model beat a home-only baseline on 7,289 later regular games, but failed simple baselines on 124 playoff games. Pitchers, rotations and lineups are not included. Known neutral games are flagged; missing venue flags retain the designated-home assumption. Pregame wins and run-based candidates remain research comparisons in the source package.

Premier League looks back at complete seasons. For each match, remove both meetings between those clubs from their final records. The other 36 matches supply points-based strength, expressed as a 38-match pace in the interface. Fit separate win, draw and loss probabilities to all 3,800 matches, including 886 draws.

Premier League: season-end strength → win / draw / loss
NBA / NHL / MLB: other-opponent season-end record → game win probability

Premier League uses later-season information: it is a retrospective relationship, not a pregame forecast. Excluding both meetings reduces circularity but does not remove hindsight. A separate draw weight is learned from real drawn matches. Single games keep draws after 90 minutes; hypothetical series introduce fair deciders.

The earliest seven seasons train the models and the last three evaluate them. These revisions reuse previously inspected evaluation seasons and remain exploratory. Soccer’s three-outcome error score is not comparable with the other sports’ binary scores. Final app coefficients refit on all ten outcome seasons; rarity uses the separate 20-season reference. See the checks below for sample sizes and results.

We match fitted neutral odds to the event model. Soccer also matches all three outcome masses, with a fixed correction to negative, zero and positive score margins. Changing scoring, opportunities, form, home or rest keeps that correction fixed: the changed odds are modeled, not measured. Within each outcome category, score shapes remain mechanistic estimates. Series assume independent games.

Games are made of opportunities.

Each team gets N independent opportunities, with a chance to produce a scoring reward. All five mean scoring levels come from the ten-season results. Final-score means include overtime or extra innings where played; NHL excludes the artificial shootout-winning goal. Opportunity counts and reward mixtures remain simplified: NBA 100 possessions; NHL 31 shots; MLB 38 batting opportunities; NFL 11 drives; Premier League 12 chances. The fitted baseline does not validate these mechanisms.

edge = baseline skill edge × sensitivity + home + rest + form
pA = logistic(logit(base scoring rate) + edge / 2)
pB = logistic(logit(base scoring rate) − edge / 2)

Home and rest controls are hypothetical event-log-odds adjustments, not fitted real-world days or points. Form is a symmetric five-point game shock. Event volatility adds reward variance while preserving its mean. More points per goal only changes units; more scoring opportunities can change predictability.

Series, draws and simulation uncertainty.

The exact model computes score distributions, then each game’s advancement probability and best-of-series outcome. Seeded Monte Carlo trials sample those game probabilities and stop when one team clinches. Increasing the number of trials reduces simulation noise, not uncertainty about the real world. The 95% interval on the cards measures Monte Carlo error only.

Single-game soccer preserves wins, draws and losses after 90 minutes. A hypothetical soccer series resolves each draw with a fair decider, as do model ties in the other sports. The series chart includes a one-game fair-decider reference; that reference differs from the soccer match headline. This does not model actual penalty shootouts. Games are independent across a series. Seeding chooses the extra home game; rest is a fixed scenario edge.

What this leaves out

Opponent schedule strength, player and roster changes, injuries, score-dependent tactics, goalie and pitcher choices, dependence between games, and actual overtime rules. Record rarity contains both skill and luck. A fitted association is not a causal explanation of why the NBA and NHL differ. In the separate-team comparison, the gap bridge first changes Team A’s record to Team B’s, holding the left sport and opponent caliber fixed. It then changes record mapping, the league baseline and scoring mechanics; format and home/rest change separately. Its contributions depend on swap order.

FROM QUESTION TO PRODUCT

Build something
you can explain.

LeagueLab began with a sports argument: why does the stronger team seem to win more reliably in basketball than hockey?

THE AUDIENCE

Curious sports fans

People who want to explore the “why” behind an upset.

THE JOB TO BE DONE

Turn an argument into an experiment

Change one assumption and understand the tradeoff.

THE PRODUCT BET

Understanding through interaction

A controllable model can make probability feel tangible.

Discovery: start with a question

The originating concept was an interactive simulation for a PM portfolio. The scope sharpened from redesigning playoff formats to separating sport mechanics from format effects. The key hypothesis: curious fans want more than a chart of upset rates; they want to see which assumptions drive the difference. This has not yet been validated with user interviews.

The defining product decisions

  1. Familiar records, explicit rarity. Season wins for NBA/MLB/NFL and season points for NHL/Premier League are compared through their own historical distributions. Rarity is a disclosed proxy for ability, not an identity.
  2. Show mechanisms separately. Scoring rate, opportunity count, event variance, and sensitivity belong to the sport layer. Series length, home seed, and rest belong to the format/context layer.
  3. Separate evidence from assumptions. Historical record scales, regular-season game fits across all teams and separate playoff checks sit alongside controlled mechanics. All five leagues lookbacks explicitly use hindsight. Sources, exclusions and separate evaluation contexts stay visible.
  4. Make the first insight immediate. Start with comparable team caliber in NBA, NHL and MLB at the same format. Inspect a matchup, then change one condition.
  5. Keep computation local. A worker prevents simulations from freezing the UI; static hosting keeps cost and operational complexity low.

A deliberate first release

Five sports, two configurable scenarios, seeded runs up to 100,000 trials, controlled comparisons, regulation draw visibility, uncertainty intervals, shareable configuration links, and JSON/CSV exports. No live scores, odds, accounts, real-team rankings, or tournament brackets.

Validation before launch

The repository includes tests for probability normalization, symmetry, compound-event moments, deterministic seeds, reward rescaling invariance, exact best-of-series probabilities, stopping rules, and simulation agreement. Interface checks cover presets, model navigation, export controls, responsive layouts, and stale result handling. These checks validate implementation. Separate-season checks evaluate the fitted relationships, with Premier League explicitly retrospective and MLB postseason transfer still weak. These checks do not validate counterfactual mechanisms.

Launch and learn

For a pilot, recruit 5–8 sports fans. Ask them to predict a counterfactual, run it, and explain the result in their own words. Observe where “strength,” “more scoring,” and “confidence interval” cause confusion. All research and success criteria below are proposed, not completed results.

Primary success signal

At least 4 of 5 pilot participants can explain the difference between changing scoring mechanics and changing series length after a five-minute session.

Supporting signals

Time to first experiment, counterfactual completion, successful result explanation, and voluntary sharing. Guardrail: no participant should interpret model probabilities as calibrated real-team predictions.

What comes next

First, improve comprehension from observed usability sessions. Then extend the five baseline checks with rolling temporal splits, series-cluster uncertainty, opponent-adjusted strength and alternative event models. Add real teams or full brackets only if they improve the core learning task. Analytics are intentionally not installed; any future measurement needs an explicit product and privacy decision.
